(soccer) A save; preventing the opposition from scoring a goal.
(zoology) The depression in a dog’s face between the skull and the nasal bones.
d.e: The stop in a bulldog's face is very marked.

d.t: A marking on a rabbit's hind foot.
d.e: The American Rabbit Breeders Association holds that the stops of a Dutch rabbit should be white from the toes to one third of the way along the foot.

d.t: (UK dialectal) A small well-bucket; a milk-pail.
(physics) The squark that is the superpartner of a top quark.
Used to indicate the end of a sentence in a telegram.
An account of real or fictional events.
d.e: The book tells the story of two roommates.

d.t: A lie, fiction.
d.e: You’ve been telling stories again, haven’t you?

d.t: (US, colloquial, usually pluralized) A soap opera.
d.e: What will she do without being able to watch her stories?

d.t: (obsolete) History.
A sequence of events, or a situation, such as might be related in an account.
d.e: What's the story with him?

d.t: (social media, sometimes capitalized) A chronological collection of pictures or short videos published by a user on an application or website that is typically only available for a short period.
(computing) Ellipsis of user story.
(chiefly US, Philippines) Alternative spelling of storey.
d.e: Our shop was on the fourth story of the building, so we had to install an elevator.

d.t: (transitive) To tell as a story; to relate or narrate about.
(ambitransitive, social media, sometimes capitalized) To post a story (chronological collection of pictures or short videos) on an application or website.
(idiomatic, Ireland, Dublin) Used as a greeting, short for what's the story?
(usually academic, transitive, intransitive) To review materials already learned in order to make sure one does not forget them, usually in preparation for an examination.
d.e: Students are expected to start studying for final exams in March.

d.t: (academic, transitive) To take a course or courses on a subject.
d.e: I study medicine at the university.

d.t: (transitive) To acquire knowledge on a subject with the intention of applying it in practice.
d.e: Biologists study living things.

d.t: (transitive) To look at carefully and minutely.
d.e: He studied the map in preparation for the hike.

d.t: (transitive) To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to dwell upon anything in thought; to muse; to ponder.
d.e:
July 10, 1732, Jonathan Swift, letter to Mr. Gay and The Duchess of Queensberry
I found a moral first, and studied for a fable.

d.t: (archaic, intransitive) To endeavor diligently; to be zealous.
Mental effort to acquire knowledge or learning.
d.e: The study of languages is fascinating.

d.t: The act of studying or examining; examination.
d.e: I made a careful study of his sister.

d.t: Any particular branch of learning that is studied; any object of attentive consideration.
A room in a house intended for reading and writing; traditionally the private room of the male head of household.
d.e: Father spends all his time in the study poring over manuscripts.

d.t: An artwork made in order to practise or demonstrate a subject or technique.
d.e: a study of heads or of hands for a figure picture

d.t: The human face, bearing an expression which the observer finds amusingly typical of a particular emotion or state of mind.
d.e: Geoffrey's face was a study.

d.t: (music) A piece for special practice; an etude.
(academic) An academic publication.
d.e: That new study on noncommutative symmetries looks promising.

d.t: One who commits a theatrical part to memory.
(chess) An endgame problem composed for artistic merit, where one side is to play for a win or for a draw.
(obsolete) A state of mental perplexity or worried thought.
(archaic) Thought, as directed to a specific purpose; one's concern.
d.e: My study was to avoid disturbing her.

d.t: (demonstrative) Like this, that, these, those; used to make a comparison with something implied by context.
d.e: I’ve never seen such clouds in the sky before.

d.t: (particularly used in formal documents) Any.
d.e: the above address or at such other address as may be provided

d.t: (degree) Used as an intensifier roughly equivalent to very much (of), quite or rather.
d.e: Unfortunately, it wasn't such a good holiday as we thought it would be.

d.t: (obsolete or dialectal) A certain; representing the object as already particularized in terms which are not mentioned.
A person, a thing, people, or things like the one or ones already mentioned.
d.e: Such is life, such as it is.

d.t: (philosophy) Something being indicated that is similar to something else.
(transitive) To help keep from falling.
d.e: Don’t move that beam! It supports the whole platform.

d.t: (transitive) To back or favor a cause, party, etc., mentally or with concrete aid:
d.e: I support France in the World Cup.

d.t: (transitive) To provide sustenance or maintenance for; to sustain in integrity or livelihood.
d.e: Mars does not currently support human habitation.

d.t: (transitive) To help, particularly financially; to subsidize.
d.e: The government supports the arts in several ways.

d.t: (transitive) To provide evidence for; to lend credibility to.
d.e: The testimony is not sufficient to support the charges.

d.t: (transitive) To serve, as in a customer-oriented position; to give support to.
d.e: The IT Department supports the research organization, but not the sales force.

d.t: (transitive) To assist or be involved with, but not be responsible for.
d.e: I support the administrative activities of the executive branch of the organization.

d.t: (transitive) To answer questions and resolve problems regarding something sold.
d.e: Sure they sell the product, but do they support it?

d.t: (transitive, software, hardware, said of electronic devices, programming languages, etc.) To be designed to provide capacity for; to work or be compatible with (a part, accessory, file type, program, algorithm, etc.).
d.e: Early personal computers did not support voice-recognition hardware or software.

d.t: (transitive, archaic) To endure without being overcome; bear; undergo; tolerate.
(transitive) To play a lesser part in the same production with (a star performer).
d.e: to support the character of King Lear

d.t: (sometimes attributive) Something which supports.
d.e: Don't move that beam! It's a support for the whole platform.

d.t: Financial or other help.
d.e: The government provides support to the arts in several ways.

d.t: Answers to questions and resolution of problems regarding something sold.
d.e: Sure they sell the product, but do they provide support?

d.t: (mathematics, in relation to a function) the set of points where the function is not zero; the closure of that set.
(fuzzy set theory) A set whose elements are at least partially included in a given fuzzy set (i.e., whose grade of membership in that fuzzy set is strictly greater than zero).
d.e: If the membership function of a fuzzy set is continuous, then that fuzzy set's support is an open set.

d.t: (commutative algebra, of a module M over a commutative ring R) The set of all prime ideals of R such that the localization of M at the prime is nonzero, denoted operatorname SuppM
Evidence.
d.e: The new research provides further support for our theory.

d.t: (software, hardware) Compatibility and functionality for a given product or feature.
d.e: This game has no mouse support.

d.t: (film) An actor playing a subordinate part with a star.
(music) An accompaniment in music.
(gymnastics) Clipping of support position.
(structural analysis) Horizontal, vertical or rotational support of structures: movable, hinged, fixed.
Physically secure and certain, non-failing, reliable.
d.e: This investment is a sure thing.

d.t: Certain in one's knowledge or belief.
d.e:
Roy: I'm 95% sure it was him.
Jen: You... you said you were 99% sure.
Roy: I'm 97% sure it was him.

d.t: (followed by a to infinitive) Certain to act or be a specified way.
d.e: Be sure to lock the door when you leave.

d.t: Certain to obtain something.
d.e: Many people book early in order to be sure of the best seats.

d.t: (obsolete) Free from danger; safe; secure.
(obsolete) Betrothed; engaged to marry.
d.e:
c. 1513-1518 (probably date written, published after 1535) Thomas More, History of King Richard III
The king was sure to Dame Elizabeth Lucy, and her husband before God.

d.t: (modal) Without doubt, certainly.
d.e: Sure he's coming! Why wouldn't he?

d.t: (archaic) Without fail, surely.
(in response to a request for help or a favour) Yes; of course.
d.e: "Could you tell me where the washrooms are?" "Sure, they're in the corner over there."

d.t: (in response to other questions) Yes; I guess; you could say that; a weak or noncommittal positive response.
d.e: "Do you like cats?" "Sure."

d.t: You're welcome; polite response to being thanked.
d.e: "Thanks for helping me with that electrical fault." "Sure. Any time."

d.t: A group or set of related things that operate together as a complex whole.
(countable, uncountable) A method or way of organizing or planning.
d.e: Followers should have a system to follow that works in their interests, not against them.
